title: UTF-8 Validation
summary: Check whether data can be partitioned into groups with these binary byte-prefix patterns: 0xxxxxxx; 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx; 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx; or 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx.
statement: Check whether data can be partitioned into groups with these binary byte-prefix patterns: 0xxxxxxx; 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx; 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx; or 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx. Return True exactly when every byte belongs to a complete valid group. This exercise checks these structural patterns only, not additional Unicode scalar-value or shortest-encoding restrictions.
constraints: Check only the listed 1–4-byte prefix patterns. A continuation byte must start with binary 10.
This exercise does not add Unicode scalar-value, surrogate, or shortest-encoding restrictions.
hints: Keep the number of continuation bytes still required by the current leading byte.
While that number is positive, accept only bytes beginning with 10. Otherwise recognize a legal leading prefix.
Prefixes 0, 110, 1110, and 11110 require 0, 1, 2, and 3 following continuation bytes. Decrement on each continuation; require zero at the end.
A leading byte is not a continuation byte. The source exercise checks these structural patterns only, so a strict Unicode decoder enforces extra rules.
editorial: A small state machine tracks the required continuation count. Masks distinguish ASCII, two-, three-, and four-byte headers. An unexpected continuation, illegal five-byte header, wrong continuation prefix, or unfinished group fails. The grading contract follows the listed bit patterns, not all real-world Unicode validity restrictions: for example [192,128] satisfies this exercise’s two-byte shape even though strict UTF-8 decoding rejects it.

tests.explanation: 11000101 starts a two-byte group, 10000010 completes it, and 00000001 is a separate one-byte group.
11101011 requires two continuation bytes. 10001100 is valid, but 00000100 is not a continuation byte.
